opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand Lean is that it's really two things at once. On one hand it's a fully featured functional programming language. You can write real software in it, and the Lean 4 compiler is actually written in Lean itself. On the other hand, it's an interactive theorem prover, and that's where the magic happens for mathematics.

The core idea is something called the Curry–Howard correspondence: propositions are types, and proofs are programs. So when you state a theorem in Lean, you're really writing down a type, and when you prove it, you're constructing a term of that type. Then a very small, trusted kernel checks that your term actually has that type. If it type-checks, the proof is correct. There's no ambiguity, no "I think the referee missed a step on page forty."

Why does that matter? Historically, mathematics has relied on social verification. You write a paper, a few experts read it, and over time the community comes to believe it. That works pretty well, but it doesn't scale, and errors do slip through, sometimes in very important results. Lean replaces that with mechanical verification. You don't have to trust the author, or even fully understand the proof yourself, to know it's correct.

The other big piece is Mathlib, the community library. It's this enormous, collaboratively built body of formalized mathematics, covering algebra, analysis, topology, number theory and so on, all consistent with each other and all checked. That's what turns Lean from a curiosity into something practical. You're not starting from the axioms every time; you're building on hundreds of thousands of verified theorems.

From our perspective, building AI for math, Lean is incredibly valuable because it gives you a perfect verifier. The big problem with language models doing reasoning is hallucination: they produce things that sound right but aren't. In Lean, you can't bluff. Either the proof checks or it doesn't. That gives you a clean reward signal for reinforcement learning, and it means that when the system says it's solved something, you can actually trust the output. So for us, Lean is the bridge between the creativity of these models and the rigor that mathematics demands.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about Lean is that it's really two things at once, and the combination is what makes it special. On one hand it's a proof assistant, a system where you can write down a mathematical statement and a proof of that statement, and the kernel checks that the proof is actually correct. On the other hand it's a genuinely good general-purpose programming language, with a real type system, good tooling, a package ecosystem, all of that.

And the reason that matters for mathematics specifically is that it turns math into something that can be verified mechanically. Historically, a proof is correct because other mathematicians read it and agree it's correct. That's a social process, and it works surprisingly well, but it doesn't scale, and it has failure modes. There have been famous cases where results were accepted for years and then turned out to be wrong. With Lean, when you have a proof that compiles, you know it's right. There's no ambiguity. The kernel is small, it's been scrutinized heavily, and either the proof type-checks or it doesn't.

Then there's Mathlib, which I think people outside the community sometimes underestimate. Mathlib is this enormous, unified library of formalized mathematics, built by hundreds of contributors, and it's growing fast. It's basically the largest coherent body of machine-checked mathematics that exists. So when you're working in Lean, you're not starting from the axioms every time, you're standing on top of real algebra, real analysis, topology, number theory, and you can build on it.

And from where I sit, the piece that gets me really excited is what this means for AI. If you want a model to do mathematics, the hardest problem is knowing whether what it produced is actually correct. Natural language proofs are hard to grade, even for experts. Lean gives you a perfect verifier. The model writes a proof, you run it, and you get a binary signal: right or wrong. That's an incredibly clean training signal, and it's the thing that lets you push these systems much further than you could if you were relying on human judgment or on another model grading the output. So Lean isn't just a nice tool for mathematicians, it's the substrate that makes verified machine reasoning possible.

astra-6.text:
I think Lean’s value is that it turns mathematics into something you can actually check with a computer. You can write down a mathematical statement, express its proof, and have the system verify that every step follows from the assumptions. That doesn’t tell you whether the statement is interesting or whether you’ve asked the right question, but it gives you a very precise notion of correctness.

And because it’s a programming language, you can write programs that help construct those proofs. You don’t have to supply every tiny step by hand. So you get this combination of a language for expressing mathematics and a framework for automating mathematical reasoning. That’s especially valuable for AI: a model can propose a proof, and Lean can check whether it actually works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Lean’s value is that it turns mathematics into something you can build on with the reliability of software. On paper, a proof is an argument that another person reads and decides is convincing. In Lean, you write the statement and the proof in a precise language, and the computer checks that the proof actually establishes the statement.

The programming-language part matters because you can define objects, write functions, and build abstractions that other people can reuse. Once you’ve proved a theorem, it becomes a component in a library, and subsequent work can depend on it without repeatedly checking the original argument.

That doesn’t mean the computer supplies the mathematical insight. You still have to figure out what to prove and why it should be true. But Lean gives you a way to make that reasoning explicit and checkable, which becomes especially valuable as the mathematics gets larger and more collaborative.
